#6640. Pamela Anderson Is a Sentimentalist at Heart

The actress on holiday traditions, motherhood, and the sentimental value of giving with Pandora.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

For Pamela Anderson, the holiday season is less about elaborate celebrations and more about appreciating life’s quieter moments. “I love the fall. I always say fall is the season of the soul,” she tells ELLE. Whether she’s tending to her garden on Vancouver Island, cooking vegetarian dishes for her family, or watching her sons establish traditions of their own, Anderson has found a new appreciation for the simple pleasures that make this time of year so special.

It’s a philosophy that extends to her approach to gift-giving. A self-described sentimentalist, Anderson prefers presents that carry a personal meaning, from family photographs to jewelry passed down through generations. And through her partnership with Pandora (Anderson is a face of the brand), she’s found a way to celebrate those connections with pieces that feel both personal and accessible.

I love the fall. I always say fall is the season of the soul. I think that’s a Virginia Woolf quote. Even in a garden, you focus more on the little things instead of being overwhelmed by so much abundance. It feels like a really special time of year. I love the fall weather and the leaves changing. It’s beautiful, especially here on the East Coast. Where I’m from on Vancouver Island, it actually looks very similar.

I absolutely love gardening. When I was home, I was cleaning up a bunch of leaves, and it feels like a workout, too. It’s nice to be outside, even in the rain. I don’t shy away from the rain, or nothing would ever get done where I’m from. I love being outside and getting my hands dirty. In this part of my life, I’m really gravitating toward that, but I’m also working a lot, so it’s a really good balance. I get to do really glamorous things, work on film and onstage, and then I go home, put my boots on, and get in the garden.

Now, the boys are usually with their wife and fiancée over the holidays. They’re building their lives and their own traditions, so I always say, “Don’t worry about me. I’m always around.” It’s nice to see them building those traditions. I’ve done a lot of hosting and party planning in my life. I’m a decorator, so I love all of that. But this year, it’s really about seeing all the traditions and things my sons have soaked up and watching them start their own lives. I’m not a pressure planner. I don’t want them to feel pressure to include me. I just say, “You guys do your thing. I’m watching, I’m observing.” It’s really special as a mom to see them so happy with their significant others. The women in their lives have great taste and love to share that with them and me.

I love cooking. I always cook all the sides, the vegetable dishes. It’s been a while since we’ve all been together for a big meal. Time is just flying by. My sons are such great cooks, too. We all have our specialties. I think I actually prefer decorating to cooking, because you set the stage. Then you can have a potluck!

I’ve given a lot of my jewelry from my lifetime to my kids and to their wife and fiancée. I like more sentimental gifts. I’m a sentimentalist, I guess. I love flowers, and this year, one of my sons just got married, but they don’t have wedding pictures of themselves. So they’re getting wedding pictures, engagement pictures, just a bunch of really sentimental things from me.

I just give my kids everything. I like to give those pieces to them so they can appreciate them while I’m here. I don’t hoard a lot of things. I’m always changing, always trying new things, and I don’t think I’m a big consumer anyway. I have special pieces that I’ve already passed on.

My mother always wants my Pandora jewelry. Every time I go anywhere, she’s asking, “Do you have Pandora? Do you have any earrings?” She loves it. My mom’s sisters and everyone just love Pandora. She loves both gold and silver, the jewels, the colors. Some of the beautiful pieces they have around the holidays, she would go crazy for. She loves it all.

I definitely wear more jewelry than I used to. It depends on what I’m wearing or where I’m going. I like to recycle jewelry. A lot of my Pandora pieces I’ve worn on different red carpets or to different special events. It’s nice for jewelry to be attainable, cruelty-free, and sustainable. Those things are so important to me. Jewelry isn’t just for the few. It’s for everybody.

When I align with somebody, I like to know that we have similar philosophies. I think it’s the small-town girl in me who never felt jewelry was in the cards for her. It’s nice to know there’s a jewelry company that’s forward-thinking and sustainable, thinking about recycling and also making it affordable. It just feels more like me. I love glamour and I love fancy things, but I think my kind of fashion is more inspirational.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6639. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6638. What Vogue Editors Are Gifting This Holiday Season

For some, gift-giving is an innate skill, but for others (myself included), it requires a little extra effort. I often find myself overwhelmed by the sheer number of options yet somehow lacking inspiration, never quite sure where to start when looking for something thoughtful and original for my loved ones. This is where being part of the Vogue Shopping team has its advantages; over the years, I’ve developed a better eye for presents that go beyond the basics. Being surrounded by people with great taste and a knack for shopping has certainly helped.

For those who may not have a fashion editor to call on for gifting ideas, I polled colleagues across Vogue’s office to see what they’re planning to give this holiday season. Their picks certainly have every type of person on your list covered—whether you’re looking for small trinkets to stuff some stockings, something to bring your favorite host at a holiday dinner, or just some little luxuries for the special people in your life. Read on to see what 26 Vogue editors and contributors are gifting this holiday season.

I live for Christmas and am always thrilled to give and receive festive gifts. I love these peppermint-striped tapers from House & Parties, Liberty print holiday crowns, and these Nutcracker crackers, and I plan to get them for myself and others. I love these cozy sock slippers from The Six Bells x Madewell and will gift them to friends for holiday mornings.

It’s often the little gifts that have the biggest impact. Something small yet thoughtful goes a long way, and our best host gifts are packed with ideas for as little as $20. From pantry supplies like tinned fish and fancy olive oil (a total crowd-pleaser) to elevated aperitivo glasses, I’ll be gifting several of these to friends, my mother, and my host for Thanksgiving lunch.

I’m keeping the bigger gifts on my list under wraps—partially for the element of surprise, mostly because I haven’t bought them yet. In the meantime, I have some smaller items on hand to give as host gifts for holiday parties (like a beautiful soap) and to weekend visitors (like a pair of nice gardening gloves for my mom). I also host a lasagna party every December and like to put tiny ornaments at each place setting so everyone can take something home besides leftovers. Toast’s hand-painted ones double as wine-glass charms, and every person gets a different one.

I’m an impassioned gifter with strong feelings about which olive oil should be on the table. Food-related gifts are my favorite to give and get, especially those I keep in my own kitchen. Incense papers are easy to tuck into a thank-you envelope alongside tea and taralli, and no one expects you to show up at their house with a fancy jar of mustard, which is exactly why you should.

These two scents from Flamingo Estate are absolutely divine; I might be addicted. The bar soap makes a great gift for anyone, from a close friend to your holiday host or even a distant relative. I love anything from Officine Universelle Buly because everything is special and you can personalize most items. The packaging is also incredible, so you don’t even have to think about wrapping them yourself—perfect for anyone who needs to travel with gifts! I am a firm believer that you don’t need to spend a lot of money on a well-received gift. Beautiful matchboxes, playful lemon squeezers, and trompe l’oeil chocolate sardines have always been fail-safe holiday presents from me, and they won’t break the bank.

Golden Door (from our Spa Guide of the best in the world!) was my most magical summer trip, and I’m gifting my sister-in-law Sarah, whose love language is cooking, its hardcover cookbook, The Golden Door Table. I love the accessories Dame Pat McGrath is creating for Louis Vuitton, and I’m buying the new Monogram Rouge Eyeshadow Pouch for myself, adding to a collection my mom started! I’m in my linen-bedding era, and my mother-in-law will get a fresh quilt from Thuma (even better for my naps when we visit!). I wore Alo Yoga out to my dad’s ranch, and now he loves the brand, so I’m getting him suited up in its soft fabrics for his winter cycling championship off-duty looks!

The holiday is fast approaching, and I’m still finalizing my gift list. A few items I’ll be buying this holiday season are a pair of shell coasters (a perfect gift for the host); a fashionable accessory for a mother, sister, or friend; a Dries Van Noten lipstick case that makes putting on lipstick a bit more exciting; and a scooter for my daughter, who has just learned how to ride one.

I’ve always been a fan of gifting items that are as functional as they are pretty. You can’t go wrong with Flamingo Estate’s personalized olive oil (adding your loved one’s name and address makes it a thoughtful housewarming gift too!) or Santa Maria Novella’s terra-cotta diffuser, my personal favorite.

As expected, my first instinct is to gift beauty goodies. I’m so blessed to test the absolute best of cosmetics, and I like to treat my loved ones to that same level of care. I always say Chanel Beauty is underrated, so it’s a good place to start when you want luxury that meets efficacy. Its gift sets are always crowd-pleasers and often arrive in a pouch you can repurpose as a toiletry bag. Otherwise, I love to gift a unique fragrance they likely haven’t heard of—like Guerlain’s 2026 debut—or little luxuries. Think: a chic leather toiletry bag (Etoile makes my favorite ones), Freja’s wine carrier, Gohar World’s tasseled comb, or Abask’s guest book.

I consider gift-giving a deadly serious ritual—not because of its materialistic nature but because it offers a chance to be particularly thoughtful when handpicking something for a loved one. As sickeningly earnest as this might seem, one of my greatest joys is making people I care about feel happy and seen. Whether the recipient has everything or has hyper-specific vibes or niche interests (I’m surely guilty of that), I have a method for finding the perfect present. An easy formula is to select a relatively ordinary item with an especially lovely or personalized design. Suddenly, an everyday object becomes a thing of beauty in their daily life. For the planner or poet, a lovely journal. (My friend Lea just gave me this for my birthday, and I adore it.) For the bookworm, a custom book stamp. For the friend that’s always touching up on the go, a gorgeous mini brush that won’t get lost in their handbag. For the decor enthusiast or as a housewarming present, a whimsical lemon squeezer. And for the glamorous friend or family member? A gorgeous lipstick case or sleek nail polish trio does the trick. I love all of the above—but when you’re not sure what to give me, fueling my original-press vinyl collection is always a win.

I love the holiday season because it’s an opportune moment to gift friends and family objects of affection that show you care. I like to think of myself as a selective, personal gifter, and I love the hunt for pieces that match each person individually. For myself, I’d love to elevate my winter wardrobe with this absolutely divine Verena Shearling Coat from Arma and the Dallen hat from Nour Hammour. Autumn Sonata makes wonderful linens and towel sets using archival prints and motifs; they transform your bathroom into an art gallery of sorts (and make excellent gifts). Though perfume is highly personal, anyone would be happy to receive a bottle of Frisson D’Hiver, described as “an audacious whisper of frost-kissed citrus and solar blooms.” These black glass coasters from Casalta are chic too.

With end-of-year holiday parties, family reunions, and dinner parties with friends filling up the calendar, I’ve found myself reaching for the tried-and-true host gift duo: flowers and a bottle of wine. But this year, I’m determined to add a little more pizzazz! Why not pair those beautiful bouquets with a fun, eclectic vase? I’m loving these options from Jonathan Adler. Or level up your favorite bottle of wine or cocktail gift with some playful glassware or an easy bottle holder.

To me, there’s no better feeling than finding the perfect gift for a loved one. I often struggle to keep gifts under wraps until the holidays, simply because I’m too excited to give them. Having grown up in a household of girls, I rarely struggle to find things my sisters or mother will love, since they are usually items I cherish or covet as well. Speaking of which, one of my best beauty discoveries of the year is Celisse’s nail products: I cannot say enough good things about them! Its polish dries in seconds and doesn’t chip for days, which is something I’ve never experienced with traditional lacquers. So someone will definitely be finding a Celisse set under the tree. And as for my dad, the only man in the house, I’ll keep adding to his espresso-cup collection.

I’m determined to have all of my holiday shopping wrapped up by Cyber Monday! I put a lot of thought into what I give each holiday season, and gifting is truly one of my favorite things to do. That said, I find the season is so much more joyful—and considerably less stressful—when I stay ahead of my lists. Flamingo Estate is always my first stop for gifts, no matter the occasion, and I’m particularly excited to give its Fig Trio set this year. This Misette candlestick is incredibly chic and comes in a range of colors, but I’ve managed to snag the red one for my mom, whose home features a red-drenched library. Maison d’Etto’s Pinehurst perfume is another lovely gift, especially for its rich, woody base notes—which make it a fitting winter fragrance. I’ve been singing Barefaced’s praises for years, and its newly launched Discovery Kit is the perfect opportunity to introduce friends and family to the brand so that they can finally see what all my fuss is about. For the phone-addicted people in my life, Brick makes a particularly clever stocking stuffer; I can think of a few people who could use one! And finally, because my husband is constantly receiving compliments on just about everything he owns from Buck Mason, I’ll be adding one of the brand’s quarter-zips to his collection this year.

I love gifting the special people in my life items that actually serve a purpose while remaining incredibly chic. Cozy winter accessories are always a go-to, like these sleek leather gloves from Agnelle and plush slippers from Ugg. A festive coffee-table book is another gift sure to delight, and this one dedicated to the legendary Grace Coddington is perfect for any fashion lover. I’m also a sucker for a beautifully scented bath oil, so why not pass that little luxury on to someone I love? And then, of course, I couldn’t help but practice a little self-love this year and include two gifts I’m either hoping to receive or might just buy for myself: Foundrae’s personalized diamond necklace and this Call It By Your Name x Minicotton tote, as I await the arrival of my baby boy early next year.

I received a match holder from my brother’s fiancée last Christmas, and at the time it was so not me. Now, I am obsessed. I have always been a lover of fire, a passion I express through my very public obsession with candles. Unfortunately, unless you’re shopping at Bath & Body Works (no judgment!), candles are expensive (and even then!). And if you burn them incorrectly (like me!), you can watch your investment go up in smoke in a matter of hours. Lately, I have become just as enthusiastic about gifting matchboxes, particularly the very chic ones from MG & Co.—a little unexpected, endlessly useful, and considerably less expensive than any high-end candle. If you’re feeling particularly generous (or confident in your relationship), go the extra mile and have the matchbox engraved. Nothing says commitment quite like putting someone’s name on a box of matches.

Gift-giving is my love language, which is great for my loved ones but not so great for my wallet! I like to give homeware items, as I find that people rarely justify buying themselves a fancy blanket or chic serveware, so they are usually overjoyed when they receive those sorts of items as a gift. My mother and I both adore anything Nickey Kehoe, so that’s my first stop when holiday shopping for her. My father is impossible to buy for, but he loves to cook, so I tend to get him fancy olive oil (you cannot go wrong with Flamingo Estate!), and who doesn’t love a new, beautiful cheese knife set for hosting season? I also discovered the brand SBE this year, so my sister and cousins will most likely receive one of its lip balms or brow gels as part of my gift to them this year. A pro tip I recently learned from a fellow gifty friend is to buy a holiday gift set, divide up the contents, rewrap them yourself, and gift the products to different friends. Genius!

I’m deep in the season of friends getting engaged, married, and buying homes, and almost everyone is keen to host large groups for special occasions. Ahead of the holidays, I’m looking for gifts for loved ones that can help them spruce up their spaces and make feeding more than just two people easier. A lot of my friends are baking bread, so the Le Creuset Dutch oven is perfect for those savory sourdough loaves. And what better way to serve some slices, along with other snacks and treats, than on gorgeous wood serving trays from Anthropologie? There’s also something to be said for adding a little whimsy around the house these days, and this magnetic photo-strip frame is perfect for that—especially for putting fun memories on display.

In my quest for a bedding refresh, I stumbled upon the perfect gift for my sister. I heard about John Robshaw from a family friend whose taste I trust endlessly; she recommended the brand’s long-lasting organic cotton percale sheets and duvet covers, which are on my wish list, but its velvet offerings felt better suited to a glamorous, cozy winter at home. So I’m planning to get my sister one of its green velvet quilted pillows, which happens to match her couch perfectly.

As someone who’s product obsessed (in both fashion and home goods), I see the holidays as my chance to share my favorite finds with the people I love. I make a point of gifting things I actually own and use because that makes them so much more personal. Below are the things I reach for constantly in my own life, from the best water filter I’ve found to delicious-smelling hand soap and my favorite multipurpose scarf. I also think everyone needs a good toiletry bag, and I’m obsessed with one from Autumn Sonata that I discovered at a local shop in Brooklyn.

To me, the best gifts come from listening to what those you love are obsessed with and figuring out how to give it to them. At a slew of parties I hosted to celebrate my new Ninja Slushi Machine, people were “joking” that they wanted to take it home; now I’m gifting the machines to friends so I will never visit a house party without fresh margs or piña coladas flowing from the spout. For my wellness-minded friends, the Biodance Collagen face masks I stocked up on in Korea will give you crazy plump skin overnight—and if they’re always comparing sleep scores, the new bands from Whoop turn the (sometimes unsightly) fitness tracker into something much more aesthetic.

I love gifting Sézane sweaters for the holidays. Who doesn’t love a cozy sweater that comes at a great price point? For stocking stuffers, I’ll be giving everyone my favorite moisturizer ever from Aestura, now sold at Sephora.

I’m a huge fan of gifts that make everyday moments feel a little more special. Whether it’s elevating an everyday essential, introducing a new hobby, setting the scene for a night of hosting, or adding a cozy touch to someone’s space, I love pieces that feel both thoughtful and useful—things they might not necessarily buy for themselves but will enjoy having.

This year I’ve found so many fun pieces on the market that would make the perfect gifts for my friends and family. From the Ro Cashmere Set by All My Love (because who doesn’t love a cozy moment during the holidays?) to the gorgeous leather notebooks from Mémoire, these finds are making holiday shopping extra exciting. Of course, while I may be shopping for others, I wouldn’t be surprised if a few of these end up in my own cart too.

Like many of us, I’ve found my screen time has gotten pretty ridiculous lately, so I’ve opted to replace scrolling with evening “sound walks” on my TP-7. I will be gifting these to my fellow audio-lover friends who want to unplug a bit, paired with the latest Nothing Audio headphones I’m constantly getting complimented on.

My partner is a silver-jewelry obsessive and has had a specific pair of Panconesi earrings on their wish list for a long time, so I will be dropping them into their stocking this Christmas!

As I’ve gotten older, candles have become one of my favorite gifts to give and receive. My friend recently recommended Keap’s Wild Fig Candle, and I will be adding it to my cart for a loved one and myself!

My younger sister told me she recently got into perfumes, so I will be sending her the Nostros discovery set so she can find the scent that’s right for her!

I’m gifting everyone Damson Madder socks this year! I know socks are sort of a blah gift traditionally, but I’m obsessed with having a particularly cute pair of rugby socks to slide on when it’s cold out (or as cold as it ever gets in LA, anyway). This female-owned London brand is committed to sustainability, which makes me feel particularly good about slipping its socks into everyone’s stocking this Chrismukkah.

#6637. Classic Stuffing

While traditional stuffing is technically supposed to be stuffed inside the turkey to cook, that isn’t actually the ideal or even recommended way to cook your Thanksgiving turkey (or stuffing). I've found that you’ll achieve much better results by cooking them separately. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath. It's my perfect version of the holiday side—I tested it again and again, so it was worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

What People Are Saying:"[It's] an excellent recipe you can tweak it for taste. I like to up the onion by half again and use a lot more fresh sage." - GreenClover

"Using a [mandoline] made the final preparation fast and easy. It was a big hit over a lovely meal. The dressing brought high praise from two trained chefs." - RedFish

As I mentioned above, sourdough bread is my go-to for stuffing. The first step is to bake it! You'll need 2 sheets, or do this in batches. You want to dry it out, so bake for 15 to 20 minutes.

While that's toasting, it's time to cook the aromatics. Melt some butter, then cook the onions, leeks, and garlic until your kitchen smells amazing and everything is softened.

Time for the liquids: Simply whisk eggs, broth, milk, and some fresh herbs in a large measuring cup. You can use a touch of red pepper for a hint of spice, which I highly recommend, but if you have a spice-averse crowd, you can skip it.

When the bread is done toasting, turn the oven temp up to 375°. Prepare a 13" x 9" baking dish by coating it with a thin layer of butter.

Time to combine it all together: In a large bowl, mix the bread, aromatics, and liquid ingredients and toss until combined. You can let this sit at room temperature for up to 1 hour if you're planning ahead. Dot with even more butter, then bake until crispy. You can serve this stuffing warm or at room temperature.

#6635. More Men Are Getting Penis Filler Than You Think

In Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life, Eric Idle sings, “Isn’t it awfully nice to have a penis?”

But, according to the new documentary Manhood, the feeling is not universal. In the film men look between their legs with nothing but shame, regret, and self-pity. The subjects’ members—particularly their perceived smallness—are problems to be solved.

Enter Bill Moore, a Dallas-based med spa operator, whose PhalloFILL penis filler procedure can supposedly add meaningful girth without surgery. The film follows his eager patients, including Ruben, an aspiring comedian and father of five, and David, a gay ex-OnlyFans star whose penis was botched by a previous filler procedure.

Director Daniel Lombroso spent years filming Moore and his patients, , slowly building trust until they opened up and (quite literally) bared all to the camera. Watching Manhood, it is clear that getting penis filler is never just about being bigger. To the patients, this procedure represents an escape from middle-aged ennui, a break from a difficult past, or a life preserver for a sinking marriage. The fast-growing, nationwide penis enlargement industry is happy to help, at $6,000 worth of filler injections per dick.

GQ sat down with Lombroso, fresh off Manhood’s breakout premiere at SXSW, to find out how he convinced a male enhancement spa to let him film inside, why the penis filler industry is booming, and who’s already getting rich off it. Manhood is available to stream on November 17.

Daniel Lombroso: That’s a great question. I think the most squeamish moment is Ruben bombing at stand-up on stage, more so than the botched penises. But, it’s funny. In real life, I am incredibly squeamish. It’s hard for me to look at surgery. It’s hard for me to look at someone using the bathroom or throwing up. There’s something about when you’re making a film, when you’re behind a lens, it gives you a level of separation. It’s sort of a mediator between you and the world. I shoot a lot of my own work, and on this project I shot some and worked with an incredible cinematographer, Vittoria Campaner. So there’s something about having that intermediary between you and the world that gave me comfort and helped me get through it. The hardest moment was the penile reconstruction, but we did not put most of that in the film.

Yeah. David, the person who gets botched, had his penis fully degloved like a banana. They had to peel back the layers and scoop out the permanent dermal filler that’s living in nodes in the shaft of his penis. That was one of the most gruesome experiences of my life. We decided to spare the audience that horror. And David is okay, thank God.

It’s tough. That was the toughest one. I also used to work at The New Yorker and I made a film on the Brazilian butt lift, which was similarly gruesome. I mean, that is one of the most gruesome cosmetic surgeries in the world. It’s a fat transfer procedure. They suck out the fat from where you don’t want it, your stomach or your arms, and stick it in where you do want it, your butt.

I filmed and watched that, and edited it on my New Yorker computer in The New Yorker newsroom for six months, and I would see David Remnick walk by and be curious and confused, and continue with his day. So it’s not my first time being in those environments, and they are hard for me personally. But something about making a film, it just gives you this level of separation that helps you get through it.

I think it’s important for people to be braced with these images. It is shocking to me how difficult it is for people to look at just a regular penis, especially straight men and older straight men. Gen X and above feel like they’re getting hit with an atomic bomb when they see a penis. Younger men, queer men, and women have always been fine, but I cannot tell you how many pitch meetings we went into where, like, the female executives love the film, the queer executives love the film. Then it gets to a straight guy at the top who is hit with one dick, and certainly one botched dick, and is out. Or he has to make sure on the record that everyone knows that he doesn’t have that problem. That happened in quite a few meetings. So I think it’s important to confront people with those images.

My business partner Kerry [Mack] joked that this is the first time I don’t have a Holocaust connection. We were looking for a penis enlargement-to-Holocaust connection, but we couldn’t find one.

I started this film three and a half years ago. At the time, we were all inundated with stories about the male loneliness epidemic. It felt almost like a cliché. I know you’ve covered it super well, and I’m sure we both grew up on Vice. It’s also something that’s really hard to show, because you don’t necessarily want to… “Condone” is the wrong word. “Platform” is also the wrong word. I hate when that word is used. But it is a cultural phenomenon that needs to be covered and discussed, and it’s very hard to do it.

I couldn’t really find a good way. Around that time, I read about the explosion in penile enhancement, and specifically, penile girth enhancement. I was less interested in penis enlargement than using that as a canvas to explore this burgeoning cultural discussion. So I called, like, every urologist in the country doing versions of it. There’s the Penuma, which is a really gnarly implant.

Yeah, Ava Kofman wrote a great story about the Penuma, which, like, pokes through and makes you bleed. I spoke to the creator of the Penuma. I spoke to people doing more permanent dermal fillers. And all of them were reticent. You know, the way I make films is I embed for many years in these environments. When I made [the alt-right documentary] White Noise, I lived on the road with white nationalists for three or four years. And for this film, I lived in clinics for two years.

So I had to find a practitioner who was open. And finally I got to Bill Moore, this very classic American character. He’s a businessman, not a doctor, and he said, “Come on down to Dallas.” So I booked a one-way ticket, and I would just sit in the waiting room and introduce myself to different patients. With a story like this, it’s really the only way. These men are so ashamed, they’re not gonna open up to a random reporter who calls them. So I knew I would have to put in a lot of time. I would just sit there, usually with my camera in a different room, and introduce myself. Sometimes they’d say, “Come back,” some would say no, some would say yes.

On those first two shoots, I met a megachurch pastor getting his penis enlarged. He’s very famous, and I cannot say who it is. A border patrol agent in the film. A father of five, an OnlyFans star, someone with brain cancer.

Super hard, and I try to be very patient. You want to push your way in at the right times and with the right people, but this is not the kind of project where you want to be coercive in any way. The last thing you want is someone saying that they were forced to appear naked in a film. So all of these men consented in different forms. Some said, “Change my voice.” Some said, “Anonymize my face.” Some said, “Just shoot my dick.” Some said, “You can shoot my face, but not my dick. I can talk about having a small dick, but don’t show it.”

There was kind of every version and permutation. But when I started to look for the main characters who could carry a film, I needed someone who was comfortable with me filming their family. Usually I’m doing vérité, like direct cinema. Really in their lives for at least a year and a half. I feel like this is front of mind for everyone now because of the Lance Oppenheim Nathan Fielder movie [You Can See Everything]. But you need someone who’s willing to invite you into their home and play the game with you, and Bill was willing to do that from the beginning.

Ruben was the next person who signed on. He’s a father of five on his second marriage. And it doesn’t go the way he might have hoped. The hardest one, I think, which speaks to your question, was David Smith. David is a pseudonym. He’s an OnlyFans star, and he had never told his story before. You would not know this from watching the film, but it actually took the entire production to get him to show his face. It was such an incredible story. I’ve never heard someone talk so openly about their botched penis and growing up evangelical and the horrors of being a male porn star.

We had a very small budget, but we saved a tiny bit of money up until the SXSW deadline. We were about to work with a face replacement company in France because that was his wish, and we thought it spoke to the theme of shame. We were starting to explore, do we hire an actor? And around that time we said, “You know what?” I used to work at The New Yorker, where you don’t really screen things. But I said, “Let’s just take a chance.” So we flew David to New York. We said, “You have no editorial control.” None of the subjects in any of my work ever have any editorial control, including my grandmother. But let’s just show him the film and see what he thinks.

And he was so blown away, he cried in the room. He called his brother, and has since opened up to his family about everything. He’s touring with the film. He came to SXSW. That took until literally a week before the premiere at SXSW, and it’s an ongoing process. He continues to become more and more open.

Yeah. I mean, it’s funny. He was a porn star. You’d think that he had such a level of exposure that he would be comfortable with this. But I think this speaks to the film. Somehow talking about your body is easier than talking about your feelings. Having to talk about his shame, his insecurity, his issues with faith, and with his parents is super, super hard for him. He needed to see the final cut to decide to go forward with it. It was the biggest gamble of my career and, thank God, it paid off.

That’s a great point. So many of the men—this takes me back now—like, I was more nervous than them. I felt like I was being potentially intrusive. I didn’t want to appear coercive in any way, as I mentioned. I wanted them to feel comfortable. But many of them felt grateful to have what you might call a third space to talk about how they feel, because most of them are not opening up to their partners, believe it or not. I don’t know how they come home with a soup can and explain that. And many of them are paying cash. There’s no credit card transaction fee. Many of them are finding ways to anonymize what they’re doing.

But at the same time, they want to talk to someone about it, which is so strange. They just don’t want the people that are part of their daily life to know, but they want Bill to know, and I think Bill deserves a lotta credit for that. He’s a queer man treating these oftentimes right-wing Texans, holding their dicks and enlarging them and making them feel comfortable.

And they wanted to talk to me, and if they wanted it to be off record, that was fine. If they wanted to be on record, that was fine. I think for many of them that was a relief. It’s so common when you work on intense stories that people start to see you as a friend or a collaborator. People see you as someone who understands their plight, and I think whenever I felt like it was starting to get there, I would remind them I’m a journalist. The world is gonna see this. Anything that is private or uncomfortable, just make sure you’re comfortable sharing before it goes in front of the world.

These guys feel so alone. Going back to White Noise, my first film, the single biggest motivator for joining those white nationalist movements wasn’t ideological conviction. I mean, some of them are gnarly racists or antisemites, but a lot of them just, like, want to be part of a club. I saw that in a lot of these men too. They just feel isolated. They want someone to talk to, and felt relieved that Bill was there to listen and that I was there to listen.

I think men, and particularly straight men—I say this as a straight man who probably struggles with this myself—have an underdeveloped sense of self oftentimes.

I’ve done these types of stories for ten years now. When I’ve interviewed women or gay men, they’ve had to think about who they are and their place in the world from such a young age. Especially queer men, from their earliest memories or certainly when they started to understand their sexuality, have had to grapple with who they are and how they appear publicly. I think that because there’s this lack of communication or lack of internal dialogue in a lot of these men, they’re internalizing so much constantly, and they’re not reaching out to those around them.

The reason I got so excited about Tuben as a character is he felt emblematic of everything we were talking about during Trump’s last re-election. You have the. disaffected conservative man who maybe voted for Trump. He would never tell me. He wouldn’t say whether he did or he didn’t, but he thinks all politicians are corrupt, and he’s living in this world on his phone that goes from Andrew Tate to porn to Nick Fuentes.

And, then here comes along a doctor, or not even a doctor, that says, “All of the things that you’re feeling can be fixed with this shot.” If you’re Ruben and you’re already feeling so alone and you haven’t spent your life thinking about who you are and your place in the world, you see a chance to fix all of your problems.

And when Ruben and Lana, his partner, had deep conversations, or when Ruben is on stage doing comedy, connecting with an audience, he feels so much better about himself. But then when he’s back to his phone, he’s feeling horribly alone, like he needs to change something. I think that’s something we all feel.

When I’m talking to my fiancée about how I’m nervous about this or that, I feel great. I feel connected. But then I go back to my phone, and I feel like shit again. So yeah, the ones who have those conversations are in a much better place.

That was by design. Every kind of man is getting this. Anecdotally speaking, Bill says that about two-thirds of the patients are straight and one-third are queer, which is surprising. Sometimes he even says three-quarters are straight, and anecdotally from my experience, that’s accurate. I’ve seen patients as young as early 20s. I mean, David was in his late teens when he got botched, or maybe right around 20 years old. He’s 24 in the film.

Yeah. I also filmed with men in their 70s. I’ve spoken to practitioners who’ve done penis enlargements for men in their 90s.

Men have been trying to enlarge their penis all the way back to the days of the cavemen, as the movie says. But now there’s this extra layer of social pressure, and technology makes it possible. It doesn’t mean that it’s safe, but it makes it possible. Every kind of man is doing this, and I felt like I needed an avatar for both.

You have the guy who’s completely seduced by bullshit online. We all know that guy. I have friends I went to college with who are that guy now. Certainly people from high school who are that guy. And then David is a little bit more heartfelt coming from OnlyFans and dealing with the scars of his experience.

There’s always something bigger. No pun intended. I really tried not to be reductive. For Bill, it was a partner who called him a “little dick motherfucker” 15 or 20 years ago, and then he started changing every part of his body. He has fake balls. He has silicone balls. He has his [fake] pecs, all of it. For David, it was growing up evangelical. For Ruben, it was dealing with abuse and being Mexican-American and things like that.

But there are ordinary people. Believe it or not, the most ordinary person I met was the megachurch pastor. He claimed he was just doing it for his wife, who he loves very much. I hope that that’s true. But almost everyone else would start that way, and then you know how it goes. It’s the old Errol Morris trick: you just kind of stay quiet and let them continue. Then they’d be like, “Oh, and also it’s this, and that, and this kid who said this fucked up thing to me 15 years ago. And by the way, my wife and I don’t have sex anymore.”

Look at implants. Whenever Dolly Parton got hers, they were sort of the medical frontier. I’m sure whoever was the version of me and you at the time was dealing with the same sort of fun, gonzo stories.

And there was probably a Dr. Loria at that time [a penis enlargement provider in the film] who was botching breast implants. It’s a lot safer now, and we know how those work. This is a—maybe unregulated isn’t the right word—but under-regulated frontier. You have people like Dr. Loria operating with impunity in Florida.

This is a guy who designs his own proprietary blend of who knows what. He literally will not tell me. It’s some kind of silicone oil. He says he’s “a hobbyist pharmacist,” and he likes to come up with his own proprietary solutions which he creates in Florida at his office. And the results you see in the film are egregious. I have yet to talk to a Loria patient who has had a positive outcome, and he is still practicing in the state of Florida.

The movie intentionally tries to leave that in a gray zone. But even the better technologies like hyaluronic acid, which is lip filler, the FDA has never said that you can inject that into someone’s dick. [But] it hasn’t said you can’t. It’s fine for off-label use. It’s all sort of the Wild West right now, and I think people don’t realize that the American medical system has all these gray areas and openings.

Bill is not a doctor. He just has to be under the supervision of a doctor, meaning a doctor came to his facility at some point and sanctioned it. Where I see the trouble is that all of these urologists who are trained to do really important medical procedures, like someone struggling with ED or who has issues after prostate cancer, they see a way to make money doing this. I saw literally dozens of urologists flock to Bill because they realize they can make a few thousand dollars in twenty minutes doing penile enhancement. Is that what they should be doing with their time? Probably not. Is that a way that they can make a lot of money? Certainly.

Business looks good. And sorry, one last point is that the penis is different also because it’s invisible. Men already don’t talk about their feelings, as you and I know. But other types of female work are visible. The media has been objectifying women from the beginning of time.

This is something that almost feels personal to men. They’re not telling their partners. Many of them say they’re doing it for themselves. Some of them literally tell me they just want it to poke bigger through their pants at the gym, or they want to show it off in the locker room. So it’s a personal choice, I think, in a way that I’m skeptical of, that’s also different from other medical procedures or kinds of plastic surgery.

[Long breath] I don’t know if you can put “long breath” in the transcript, but… I believe in a kind of documentary filmmaking that doesn’t impose a takeaway. I think we now live in this streamer era where movies are designed to be “two screen” documentaries. It’s a Netflix term, where you can fold laundry [while watching], and they tell you every third of the movie what it’s about and what the takeaway is. The movie is not pro-penis enlargement. It’s not anti-penis enlargement. It’s using that as a canvas to explore all of these things and I think that’s where I like to start. That said, I would not recommend my friends do it. Bill tried to get me to do it, by the way.

Many times. And I am willing to do anything for my stories, like be in bed with Nazis for years or whatever the fuck. I was not willing to do that. The simple fact is that this is a medical gray area. No one knows how safe it is. Filler migrates, and the problem is in your penis.

Whoever that friend is, I would be like, “What issue are you having in your marriage, with your kids, with your self-esteem, with your body?” And I would really welcome the chance to get close to that friend again, you know? As you get older, people are around less, people have kids, people are also more isolated. They’re in their family. And those moments actually can lead to incredible breakthroughs when your friend is like, “I’m scared that my dick is not good enough.”

I would have just been gifted with the most exciting conversation that I’ve had in months, and I would welcome that. We would go on a hike, or have a beer, and talk about why he doesn’t like his dick. I think we as a society would be better if we did that more often.

#6634. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

The pre-holiday party season is in full swing—and if you needed any further proof, one just had to look around the jam-packed dining room at The Mark on Monday evening. Not since the first Monday in May has the popular hotel been so thronged with famous faces at the beginning of the work week. #6632. Green Bean Casserole

Green bean casserole belongs on every Thanksgiving spread. If you're scrambling to figure out how to perfect the classic side dish, look no further. I ditched the cream of mushroom soup for a homemade cream sauce and fresh sautéed mushrooms, but don’t worry—this dish is still super-simple to make. You only need 8 ingredients and a little over an hour to make it. Keep reading on for my top tips to make this classic side dish the best it can be:

What People Are Saying:"Once you have this, you'll never be able to go back to the Campbell's gray sodium laden sludge & soggy canned green beans recipe! This is amazing! Your whole family will change their minds about green bean casserole." - CyanCarrot

"This is the best green bean casserole I've ever made! It was easy enough that I could read it through twice, and then just make the dish without having to refer to the text of the recipe! It turned out great, my family ate it up! Without using a can of condensed soup, I could control the amount of salt...this made from scratch sauce tastes more mushroomy than a can of condensed soup!" - GreenBike

The very first step is blanching the green beans. This may seem a little fussy, but it's the best way to start cooking the beans to preserve their crispy texture and bright green color as they continue to bake in the oven. It's easy, but just requires a little setup. Cook the beans in salted water for a few minutes, then immediately transfer to a bowl of ice water to stop the cooking process. That's it!

On to the aromatics! This is what takes this casserole truly over the top. Cook sliced onions in butter until just starting to soften, anywhere from 7 to 10 minutes.

Add the mushrooms and let everyone get to know each other. Make it even better by adding some garlic; in my opinion, the more, the merrier. Your kitchen will smell amazing. Pour the aromatics into the bowl with the blanched beans.

Time for the sauce. No need to wipe out the pot, just melt a stick of butter, then toast the flour.

Slowly pour in the milk and whisk, letting the sauce come to a simmer, until nicely thickened. Be sure to taste for salt and pepper.

Add to bowl with beans, stir to combine, then transfer to a 13" x 9" baking dish. Spread in the dish, then bake until everything is bubbly, which should take just 30 minutes.

Time for the fried onions! Return to the oven and bake until the onions are just warmed through, about 5 minutes more.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Save some time (and oven space) on the busy holiday by making this Thanksgiving side ahead of time. Simply assemble the casserole (without the fried onions), cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for up to 4 days or until you're ready to bake!

Some tips: Make sure to let it cool to room temperature before baking, or add a couple of minutes to your timer to adjust to the colder temperature. Whatever you do, DON'T forget to add the fried onions until after the first round of baking. If they're added before refrigerating, they'll get soggy instead of having that signature crispy crunch.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container (or cover your casserole dish with storage wrap) before refrigerating. This side will last up to 4 days refrigerated (look through our Thanksgiving leftovers ideas for some creative inspo for what to do with them), and leftovers can be reheated in the microwave or oven.

#6631. Joaquin Phoenix Wasn’t Thinking About 'Her' When He Filmed This Intelligent Eyewear Campaign

It feels like a scene out of a sci-fi movie: Joaquin Phoenix is standing across from me, instructing me to speak into his eyeglasses in a foreign language.

“Let’s see what happens,” the Oscar winner says. “It could be any language.”

The idea we’re testing here is whether the glasses Phoenix is wearing—a dark-rimmed pair from the South Korean luxury eyewear brand Gentle Monster’s new Intelligent Eyewear collection—could live-translate these words into English. This is one of the glasses’ capabilities the actor was most delighted to discover while he was shooting their campaign film directed by another Oscar winner, Jonathan Glazer. The glasses were crafted in partnership with Google and Samsung, and feature AI-powered technology.

Joaquin Phoenix in the Jonathan Glazer-directed campaign spot.

The last time Phoenix appeared in a fashion campaign, it was 1997 and he was modeling moody suits for Prada. This time around, he stars in the Glazer-directed spot that Phoenix says was partially inspired by the 1969 documentary Salesman, in which vendors travel across New England selling Bibles. In the Gentle Monster ad, Phoenix’s character—who has an intense, quasi-manic energy—ventures into an unnamed hotel, where he falls into a deep sleep and meets colorful, large creatures at the end of a hallway. (One might even call them…Gentle Monsters.) Per a press release, the “intelligent eyewear becomes his way of understanding their language and communicating with them, opening up unexpected possibilities for connection.”

Phoenix had wanted to work with Glazer for a long time. “I’ve known him for years, and when we all approached him, we came up with this really interesting and offbeat idea that just [had so] much mood. He just gets super excited and inspired,” the actor says. During the shoot, the Zone of Interest filmmaker kept the camera rolling for prolonged periods of time, encouraging Phoenix to harness different emotions. A moment in the ad might last for “30 seconds, but we shot for 15 minutes,” he explains. “A whole range of things are happening in those 15 minutes, things that we were trying.”

In an email, Glazer reiterated that he was glad to have had a reason to work with Phoenix: “The first image I had was him asleep, maybe dreaming, with the glasses all wonky across his face. The rest kind of grew from there,” the director said.

When I meet the actor last Wednesday at 23 Wall Street in Manhattan—where Gentle Monster has staged an enormous activation for the Intelligent Eyewear launch, complete with fake horses with wagging tails and huge surreal sculptures—it’s hard not to think about his turn in the 2013 film Her, one of the most prophetic AI movies of our time. In the Spike Jonze near-future drama, Phoenix’s character, Theodore Twombly, chats with and subsequently falls for an AI-powered operating system voiced by Scarlett Johansson. If 2011’s Contagion foreshadowed the COVID-19 pandemic, Her’s depiction of chatbots feels eerily similar to the world of ChatGPT dots, Meta Muses, Claude Duets, and Gemini Sparks that we’re beginning to grow accustomed to.

Phoenix and his partner, actress Rooney Mara, wearing Intelligent Eyewear at the Gentle Monster event in Manhattan.

When I ask Phoenix if filming the campaign made him think of Her, he shrugs. “I wasn’t. It seems like I should have,” he says. “It’s funny because I think that sometimes films have more of, maybe, an impact on the people that view them than for me, but I hadn’t thought about that. Somebody just made a joke about it actually, and I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re right.’”

Phoenix, who most recently starred in 2025’s politically tinged neo-Western Eddington, leaves on his Intelligent Eyewear glasses—which are Gemini-embedded, sleek, and thick-rimmed—while we speak.

“The thing is,” he says, “I’m not even aware that I’m wearing them.”

#6629. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6628. I Tried Taco Bell’s New FLAMIN’ HOT Menu Items To See If They Really Bring The Heat

One of these could've used a few extra sauce packets.

I'll try just about anything Taco Bell puts on its menu, and whatever I order usually ends up drenched in hot sauce. So when I heard the chain was adding a new FLAMIN' HOT offering (and bringing back a punchy fan favorite), I was curious whether they'd finally give me enough spice to leave those packets alone. I like my food hot enough to get a few beads of sweat forming on my nose, and with a name like FLAMIN' HOT, I don't think that's asking too much.

There were two contenders: the returning FLAMIN' HOT Grilled Cheese Burrito ($5.49), which I'd missed during its first run, and the brand-new FLAMIN' HOT Mini Taco Salad ($2.49). Both feature Fritos FLAMIN' HOT, so I figured I was in for some decent spice. Here's how that worked out.

I love a good taco salad, especially when the bowl itself is edible. But my first impression of this mini version was that it looked like a pretty ordinary Taco Bell salad. And after a few bites, I wasn't finding much to convince me otherwise.

You've got seasoned beef, refried beans, lettuce, tomatoes, cheddar, and Creamy Chipotle sauce tucked into a crispy flour tortilla bowl. Beneath everything was a layer of reddish rice, which Taco Bell says is seasoned with FLAMIN' HOT Fritos. I could definitely see the color, but whatever was making that rice spicy wasn't doing much for my taste buds.

And speaking of Fritos, I'm still trying to figure out where mine went. They're supposed to be in there, but I genuinely couldn't tell whether they'd been included in my particular serving. I would've loved more of the chipotle sauce, too, because the other ingredients seemed to overpower whatever heat was hiding underneath.

The shell itself was fine, although a little bland and greasy. I’m still pro-taco salads, but I just wish the spice had been more noticeable—especially with a name that makes such a big promise.

The returning burrito is stuffed with seasoned beef, spicy rice, crunchy FLAMIN' HOT Fritos, nacho cheese sauce, sour cream, and Creamy Chipotle sauce. And because Taco Bell clearly believes there's no such thing as too much cheese, the entire thing gets a three-cheese blend grilled onto the outside of the tortilla.

I took a pretty substantial first bite, making sure to get into those Fritos and all its FLAMIN’ HOT components. The nacho cheese had that gloriously gooey, movie-theater quality (complimentary), while the rest of the fillings worked together much better than they had in the salad. There's a lot happening inside this thing, and I was enjoying every bit of it.

Most importantly, I could actually taste the heat. There was a satisfying punch of spice, followed by that little tickle at the back of my throat that tells me something's doing its job. I wasn't desperately reaching for a drink, but the burrito had enough kick to make me happy.

I even went back for another bite of the mini taco salad afterward, and it tasted better with the burrito's lingering heat still in my mouth. Who knew it needed a little help from its menu companion?

Ultimately, the burrito is the one I'd order again. The mini taco salad has potential, and for $2.49, I wouldn't be opposed to giving it another shot. But next time, I'm bringing the extra hot sauce packets it should've saved me from needing.

#6624. Drinking Tea Too Hot Could Be Bad For Your Health—Here's What To Know

Your morning cup might benefit from a little patience.

There’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health. A recently published study followed nearly half a million adults in China for almost a decade, examining how tea-drinking habits related to their health. Researchers found that regular tea drinkers had a lower risk of vascular disease than non-tea drinkers. But one major caveat emerged: Those who reported drinking their tea “burning hot” had a higher risk of vascular disease.

According to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease. But don't give up your daily tea habit quite yet. “This study is interesting, but we don't have a proven biological explanation yet,” Dr. Niraj Patel, medical director at Clara, says.

Dr. Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.

“It doesn’t look like this study has any proposed mechanism for why burning hot tea would increase the risk of cardiovascular disease,” she explains. “However, we do know that drinks that are too hot can increase the risk of esophageal cancer by creating local injury and damage.”

That concern is supported by the World Health Organization's cancer research agency, which has classified drinking beverages hotter than 149°F as probably carcinogenic to humans. The classification specifically concerns esophageal cancer, though, so it doesn't explain the connection to vascular disease identified in the new study.

The study didn’t identify a specific temperature at which drinking tea becomes detrimental to vascular health. And although researchers found an association between drinking extremely hot tea and vascular disease, that doesn't necessarily mean one causes the other.

ScienceDaily also notes that drinking tea at extremely high temperatures may diminish some of the health benefits associated with regular tea consumption.

Azarcon believes further research into tea's chemical makeup and how it may change at different temperatures could help answer some of the remaining questions.

"I'd say enjoy your tea, but don't feel like you need to drink it while it's scalding hot,” Patel suggests. “There's a difference between brewing tea with hot water and actually drinking it at that temperature. Letting it cool for a few minutes is an easy precaution and doesn't require giving up something you enjoy."

So while I don’t plan on giving up my tea habit any time soon, I am definitely making extra sure that I let my cup sit out a little longer before taking that first sip.

#6623. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6622. How to Style a Bed, According to Interior Designers

As the days grow shorter and the temperatures drop, there’s nothing quite like knowing there’s a warm, welcoming bed awaiting you at home to usher in a good night’s sleep (followed, ideally, by a long, languorous morning). If ever there were a season that invites spending more time in bed, it’s this one—so it’s high time to put a little effort into creating your perfect set-up.

“You want the bed to welcome you upon walking into the room,” says Patrick Williams, founder of Berdoulat. “I believe there’s a balance to be struck between considered juxtaposition of fabric and color, and an inviting, relaxed, laissez-faire look.” The question of how to make a bed seems simple enough—after all, it’s a task one masters as a child—but to get it to the next level, a few extra steps can go a long way. It’s the difference between good-enough and hotel-quality.

With this in mind, we tapped a few interior designers to see how the pros style their beds; here’s what works, what doesn’t, and what will take bedtime from functional necessity to daily luxury.

A bedroom at a home in San Francisco designed by Katie Monkhouse.

The prospect of a bed without a duvet may seem like a step too far, especially in colder climates—but Heidi Caillier insists it’s worth reconsidering. “I do not use duvets or comforters,” she says. “I don’t like how lumpy they are and personally find them uncomfortable to sleep under.” Her secret lies in layering: start with a crisp bottom sheet, then build warmth and texture with quilts and blankets in a mix of colors and patterns. “It feels more collected and less perfect,” she says.

If you’re not yet willing to part with your duvet, then try layering pattern instead. Per Williams: “A bed with solely one-colored bedding can feel rather ominous to me, so I love varying texture and color or tone. There is a lovely moment of discovery when getting into the bed and seeing, let’s say, a ticking stripe pink and blue sheet beneath an otherwise very neutral ochre linen set.” A floral pattern–as with Anthropologie’s rose-printed sheet–works well here.

A bedroom in Brooklyn designed by Heidi Caillier.

While some like a bed well-endowed in the pillow department, most of the experts I spoke to agreed that too many is not a good look. If the bed is a double, Cailler’s styling formula is typically four sleeping pillows (two on both sides) placed one on top of the other, plus one single decorative pillow in front. “I prefer to keep these smaller and strongly dislike the large European pillows,” she says.

You also can’t go wrong with a single long lumbar cushion—see, the below velvety ochre one from Soho Home. With her clients, Katie Monkhouse keeps things minimal with just one large lumbar pillow and a throw on the end of the bed: “This combination is usually enough to make it feel stylish but inviting,” she says. “Try pulling the top blanket up and over the sleeping pillows and then rest the long lumbar in front for a clean, minimal look.”

Great for both warmth and aesthetic appeal, quilts, bedspreads, and eiderdowns are having somewhat of a moment. “American designers have always had a thing for English country style and creating that layered, cozy, slightly nostalgic look; things like eiderdowns and quilts fit into that well,” says Cinny Aumonier. “The combination of down and detailed stitching creates a plump, sculptural quality that gives the bed real presence.” Choose a minimal solid color or something in a punchier pattern, like JW Anderson’s tangerine-and-tomato blanket, to give this traditional textile a mod spin.

As for the designer-loved sources? “I love some of the quilts from John Derian and Nickey Kehoe and personally use a quilted one from Parachute Home all the time,” says Caillier. “I also love vintage—I’m always looking for new and interesting bedding resources. The more mismatched the layers on a bed, the better.”

A Belgravia bedroom designed by Buchanan Studio.

Try framing the bed with either a fabric canopy or curtains—see the latter in the peaceful room above from Buchanan Studio. “We wanted to soften the geometry of a perfectly symmetrical master bedroom and bring in a sense of calm and sensuality, so we added curtains on an oversized curved curtain pole—when drawn, they almost create a room within a room, and when open, they still offer a cocoooned and private world within the main space,” co-founders Charlotte and Angus Buchanan explain. It wasn’t a simple installation, but the effort was worth the squeeze.

A fabric canopy is a little easier to execute, but no less impactful. Tori Murphy created her best-selling line of striped canopies as a way to bring texture and warmth to the bedroom. “A simple trick to recreate a similar effect is to hang a curtain rail behind your bed—above the headboard if you have one—and drape your chosen fabric from it. It looks incredibly striking but is also deceptively easy,” she says. Even a plain cotton or linen can bring a sense of serenity to your space.

As for those in the market for something more opulent—a four poster bed will definitely fit the bill.

The resounding advice from every expert? “Don’t overcomplicate it. Too many decorative elements can make a bed look fussy and too staged,” says Monkhouse.

Williams agrees: “I am not a fan of overly dressed beds where one must deconstruct and remove piles of cushions to gain entry,” he says. Blankets, quilts, and cushions are there to be used; they’re not purely for show.

For the ultimate hotel-worthy comfort, the Buchanan design duo recommend starting with an excellent quality mattress and mattress topper—the latter should be between two and three inches thick for a cloud-like feel—and picking the right basics from there. Coyuchi, Parachute, and Brooklinen all make reliably great sheet sets.
