#6467. A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

On a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she said. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a big bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”

Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur said. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”

Over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “New Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503

The Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

Venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary new guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592

Chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in New York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

“You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

If, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

In 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

You’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

Be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

We found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906

On Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers quickly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580

Across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

Pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

At Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

Among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

The Colmado, Bur says, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

At the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, big sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”

One couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”

Smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter said, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

Pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

At Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

Among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

The Colmado, Bur says, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

At the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, big sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”

One couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”

Smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter said, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

#6466. Naomi Hand Scrub Gets Rid of Garlic Smells and Softens Your Skin

I’m a big proponent of indulging in little luxuries—especially if they’re for my home, where I live and work. I acquire fresh flowers weekly, I don’t wait for special occasions to burn expensive candles, and my hand soap smells like it came from a fancy hotel.

Until very recently, I kept my luxuriously scented soaps in both my bathroom and my kitchen. The latter, I realize, isn't the most practical choice—after cutting onions or garlic, a pleasant fragrance doesn’t so much mask the smell as combine with it. But sticking a pump bottle of Dial or SoftSoap next to my sink doesn’t exactly fit the bougie-divorcée apartment vibe I’m going for.

Now I don’t have to choose because somebody finally developed fancy hand soap just for cooks. And it’s really nice.

Naomi After-Cooking Hand Scrub is the creation of an enthusiastic home cook whose girlfriend couldn’t stand the garlic smell that lingered on his hands. Like me, she also happened to have a thing for premium hand soaps. And I’m so glad she did because this stuff really is a dream.

The selling point for anyone who regularly chops alliums is that it uses bread yeast enzymes to neutralize odors. It also exfoliates your hands with tiny (though not uncomfortable) pieces of volcanic rock and keeps your skin soft with olive oil esters.

But the thing that has me swooning is the fragrance: a combination of bergamot, sandalwood, and black pepper. It’s subtle but feels rich, and I prefer it to Aesop’s Resurrection Hand Wash. Naomi’s After-Cooking Hand Scrub happens to be about half the price of Aesop’s Hand Wash too.

After-Cooking Hand Scrub, Bergamot & Pepper

Before I finished my first bottle, I ordered a second. Then I realized I should have ordered more because this is absolutely going to be my new go-to dinner party host gift.

If fancy smells aren’t your thing for whatever reason (allergies, sensitivities, or disliking nonfood scents in the kitchen), you’ll be happy to know that Naomi also offers a fragrance-free option alongside two scented soaps. It offers the same luxe feel as their scented soap, but instead of volcanic rock, it exfoliates with tiny bits of biodegradable jojoba wax.

And if you love the scent as much as I do, Naomi also makes a scrub-free hand soap that smells just as lovely. My bathroom sink is next.

#6463. Glace Drops At-Home Version Of Its Viral Hot Chocolate

All the chocolate, none of the NYC lines.

If you've spent any time on food TikTok, you've probably come across Glace's famous S'mores Hot Chocolate. The New York City dessert shop has become a social media sensation thanks to its ridiculously rich hot chocolate, complete with a thick ring of toasted marshmallow fluff around the cup and hefty scoop of whipped cream to top it off. And now you won't have to book a trip to Manhattan and stand in line just to try it.

Glace has officially launched its first-ever at-home hot chocolate mix, giving fans across the country the opportunity to recreate its signature drink without leaving their kitchens. And given how popular the in-store sensation has become, I'm guessing plenty of people will add this easy-to-duplicate version to their holiday wish lists.

Founded by Sasha Zabar in 2023, Glace first opened on New York City's Upper East Side, where its over-the-top S'mores Hot Chocolate quickly became the star of the menu. The drink, which features rich drinking chocolate surrounded by a toasted marshmallow rim, has attracted plenty of attention online.

Since then, the brand has continued to dominate social media with other over-the-top menu items like its à la mode Warm Brownie Pudding Cake and Matcha Fudge Sundae, and has also expanded with a seasonal holiday truck at Rockefeller Center and Glace Candy, a neighboring shop specializing in gummies, chocolates, and other sweets.

But its newest launch means you don't have to live anywhere near New York to get a taste of at least one of its viral treats.

The new Signature Hot Chocolate Mix costs $19.99 and comes with six individual sachets, each containing the same hot chocolate recipe served at Glace's shops.

According to the brand, the mix is made with ground chocolate and A2 milk powder, without the cornstarch or powdered fillers commonly used in conventional hot chocolate mixes. The result is designed to deliver the same rich, glossy consistency that made the drink famous.

Preparing it is pretty straightforward: Simply whisk the mix over medium-low heat on the stovetop until it transforms into a thick, decadent drinking chocolate. Sadly, the at-home version doesn’t come with the shop’s signature marshmallow rim...at least, not yet.

Glace says it's planning to release its signature marshmallow fluff separately, allowing customers to eventually recreate the full experience at home, toasted marshmallow rim and all. The brand hasn't announced an official release date for the fluff, but we're keeping an eye out.

For now, the hot chocolate mix is available for pre-order on Glace's website, with shipments expected to begin in early December.

Neuroscientists say people can be "trained" to recognize when they're dreaming — in other words, lucid dreaming may be an acquirable skill.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During dreams, bizarre scenes you encounter can seem as tangible as reality; you feel as though you're really flying through the sky or being chased through a jungle of bright-purple trees. But in special cases, people realize they're in the midst of a dream as it's unfolding.

Called lucid dreaming, this phenomenon occurs when we suddenly regain our capacity for metacognition, or thinking about our own thoughts, in the middle of a dream. Lucid dreamers can sometimes even control the content or trajectory of their dreams. Now, researchers claim that they've found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they're awake.

In a study involving a few dozen participants, the scientists found that repeating this training twice a week for a month significantly increased how often participants experienced lucid dreaming. They say the approach could have practical applications as an intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder — but those applications are theoretical, for now.

If you could learn how to lucid dream, would you? Let us know in the poll below, and add your thoughts in the comments.

#6460. Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series will dive deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community. She has showcased her adventures and recipes as @blackforager since 2018 (with millions of curious followers across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube) and now in her debut cookbook, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! This comprehensive guide to finding and cooking with ingredients from your backyard or nearby forests and fields is organized by season and anchored by Nelson’s vibrant personality and boundless energy, encouraging readers to get out of their comfort zones and educate themselves on edible plants hiding in plain sight.

Nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family. “You have to finish growing first!” Nelson recalls her mom saying. Nelson ate meat products to keep from wasting food her parents prepared until she was 12, when she decided to start packing her own lunches. “It was a lot of undressed Boca burgers and French fries. It was a bleak time,” she admits with a laugh. She went fully vegan at 24 and hasn’t looked back.

I am not a very outdoorsy person, but I was captivated by the whimsical way Nelson goes about foraging and sharing online, and even more so after chatting with her on a recent Zoom call. When I asked for easy gateway foraging ideas, she immediately suggested field garlic or onion grass: “I am a biased party, because that is the first forageable that my mom taught me. Once you notice it, you see it everywhere, and it has a foolproof test, which is the smell test. If you break it and it doesn’t very fragrantly smell of onions and garlic, you have the wrong plant. Easy, easy!” She recommended looking for little purple flowers or round pink spiky balls, and on my next walk with my dogs, I spotted some. I haven’t picked and cooked with any yet, but now I’m on the lookout (and smell-out) for this abundant allium and plan on pairing it with the maitake bacon recipe from her book. Nelson suggested making a “BLT-adjacent sandwich with whatever mild greens are in season, a slice of tomato, and maitake bacon on toasty sourdough.”

Whether you’re a foraging beginner or an expert, Nelson’s edition of Amused Bouche will be equally eye-opening and mouthwatering. Read on for her adventures and misadventures in the fields and in her home kitchen.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

I love a tofu scramble and mixing in whatever is in season, and I bring home mushrooms, greens, and aromatics. In the springtime, it’ll be ramp leaves and oyster mushrooms. In the summer, it’s chanterelle and bicolor bolete with some nodding onion flowers from my front yard. As we move into winter, I’m thankful that we get enoki mushrooms pretty consistently all throughout the season in the woods. I do a combo of firm silken and super-firm tofu because I want the best of both worlds. Eggs don’t just have one texture; the whites and yolks are different, and I always want to try to get as close to eggs as I can with my tofu textures. I’m perpetually on a search for a forageable legume that I can make my own tofu with. One of my friends, Jesse Akozbek (@feralforaging), makes tofu with black walnuts.

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

The first thing that I remember cooking is baking cakes with my dad—usually just a basic frosted vanilla cake. My mom used to be a cool head-honcho character at Procter & Gamble, and she would be gone for two or three weeks at a time for work. We’d bake the cake the night before [she got back], frost it, and then just before she came home, we’d leave the cake out and hide.

I broke out my food mill because I went a little overboard harvesting cornelian cherries with my fiancé this year. They’re fun to harvest, and we brought a step stool to reach more and ended up going home with a couple gallons of fruit. It’s all fun and games until you see them all on the counter and realize they’re gonna go bad so I gotta figure out what I’m doing with all of this. I thought of doing a glacé cornelian cherry like I’ve done with chestnuts before, but the water content of the cherries is so high that when I simmered them in a sugar syrup, they just disintegrated and disappeared. I tried to stir it carefully, but it all just turned into goo. I fished them out with my little spider, put them in my food mill, and ground it. They have big ol’ pits on the inside, and I am not trying to eat any of those. It was an applesauce consistency in the end, but like what if applesauce had dreams? What if applesauce was the star of a Studio Ghibli movie? I made cornelian cherry shortcakes with it, and my fiancé was like, “So I’ve had three…” and we realized that when you eat a lot of fruit and fiber at once, you remember it later. I also saved the flavored syrup that was created after straining out all of the goopy fruits, and I am saving it specifically for making Shirley Temples!

My favorite way to treat myself is getting dinner with my fiancé at Agni, an amazing Bengali American fusion restaurant here in Columbus, led by my friend, chef Avishar Barua! They have these french fries that take three days to make, and I—no joke—dream about them sometimes.

Marie Viljoen’s Forage, Harvest, Feast is the cookbook that showed me as a recent college graduate that foraging, the weird thing I’ve been doing since childhood, could become such elevated cuisine. It’s absolutely stunning, and she is a recipe and photography genius—she does it all! I remember checking that book out from the library for the first time and my jaw dropping at how she used foraged foods in ways I had never even let myself consider. She gets shouted out in my cookbook because I used a few of her recipes as a jumping-off point then over time I started changing things to make them my own. A decade later, it becomes something different but still has the heart of that original recipe, like my milkweed nectar is definitely the child of her milkweed cordial! Her book was eye-opening for me even before I knew this was what I was going to end up making my career, back when it was something I just did because I loved it and I was a poor recent grad. A really great way to spruce up a 59-cent pack of ramen is wild greens and mushrooms!

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

I keep doing this thing where I start fermenting drinks and then travel, which is dumb. Don’t do that! My most explosive ferment was actually not mine, it was a gift from fellow foraging friend Gabrielle Cerberville (@chaoticforager). She very kindly brought me a bottle of her wild plum wine, and I did not put it straight into the fridge because I was not using my noggin. Three days later, I went to open it to pair with dinner, and it was like my world was in slow motion and it was just a geyser everywhere! Wine on the ceiling, wine on the walls, a lot of wine on the floor, a lot of wine on me. I cleaned it up sadly, shooing my pets away. No drunk pets! I also had a milkweed cordial explode, which meant I had to scrub sticky pink off every single thing in the refrigerator. Do not recommend it.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

I grew up in the Cincinnati area, so there will be a soft spot in my heart for Cincinnati chili forever. It’s just ingrained within me. Thankfully Skyline has vegan rice and beans using the same spices that you can also put onto pasta like a wild Ohioan. That will always taste like a Friday evening with my dad, because my mom is from New England and famously hates Cincinnati chili. I think calling it a chili was maybe its biggest downfall—when you learn about the history behind it and how it’s actually the child of a Greek meat sauce, suddenly the spice palette makes so much more sense. I think people would be so much cooler with that, but everyone’s expecting Tex-Mex chili, and that is not what you are signing up for!

When you’re playing dinner party DJ, what’s spinning?

There was a podcast I was obsessed with called The Dinner Party Download a decade ago, and I named my playlist after that. It has been evolving throughout the past 10 years and has Mitski, which I know feels sad for a dinner party but it’s mellow, some alt-J, Bill Withers, The Contours. A lot of Motown-era music, like The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, The Four Tops, Staple Singers. And then Janelle Monáe, Kate Nash, “Rhapsody in Blue” by George Gershwin is thrown in there. I go all over the place, but I think it creates a general buzzy atmosphere. I don’t want it to necessarily be as dancey as a dance party, but I also don’t want people to fall asleep, either.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

I really love plating things and cutting things into fun shapes and making them look pretty. I took a cooking class in Japan with Elizabeth Andoh, a very prolific cookbook writer, a couple of years ago, and after my fiancé and I walked out of it, we were just like, “Dang, our food’s real ugly!” A huge part of her class was how much presentation matters and how the first way that you are consuming the food is with your sight, with your eyes, so why not make it look cute?

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

While my fiancé and I were in Florence for a friend’s wedding, we knew that Italy, historically, was not the easiest place to be vegan. You can find things but maybe not that many things, and maybe not the things that look as good as the things everybody else is eating. So I was big sad the entire time until we stumbled into a tiny hole-in-the-wall vegan restaurant called Il Vegano. We found it on Google by searching “vegan restaurants near me,” and it had the best pasta with tomato sauce and tiramisù that either of us have ever had. Mind you, my fiancé is not vegan and very much could still eat real tiramisù and did on that trip. And the night ended with us essentially begging in broken Italian for the head chef to write a cookbook. We waddled back to our hotel saying it was the best meal we’ve ever had.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Hungry for even more stories to sink your teeth into?

I remember checking that book out from the library for the first time and my jaw dropping at how she used foraged foods in ways I had never even let myself consider. She gets shouted out in my cookbook because I used a few of her recipes as a jumping-off point then over time I started changing things to make them my own. A decade later, it becomes something different but still has the heart of that original recipe, like my milkweed nectar is definitely the child of her milkweed cordial! Her book was eye-opening for me even before I knew this was what I was going to end up making my career, back when it was something I just did because I loved it and I was a poor recent grad. A really great way to spruce up a 59-cent pack of ramen is wild greens and mushrooms!

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

I keep doing this thing where I start fermenting drinks and then travel, which is dumb. Don’t do that! My most explosive ferment was actually not mine, it was a gift from fellow foraging friend Gabrielle Cerberville (@chaoticforager). She very kindly brought me a bottle of her wild plum wine, and I did not put it straight into the fridge because I was not using my noggin. Three days later, I went to open it to pair with dinner, and it was like my world was in slow motion and it was just a geyser everywhere! Wine on the ceiling, wine on the walls, a lot of wine on the floor, a lot of wine on me. I cleaned it up sadly, shooing my pets away. No drunk pets! I also had a milkweed cordial explode, which meant I had to scrub sticky pink off every single thing in the refrigerator. Do not recommend it.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

I grew up in the Cincinnati area, so there will be a soft spot in my heart for Cincinnati chili forever. It’s just ingrained within me. Thankfully Skyline has vegan rice and beans using the same spices that you can also put onto pasta like a wild Ohioan. That will always taste like a Friday evening with my dad, because my mom is from New England and famously hates Cincinnati chili. I think calling it a chili was maybe its biggest downfall—when you learn about the history behind it and how it’s actually the child of a Greek meat sauce, suddenly the spice palette makes so much more sense. I think people would be so much cooler with that, but everyone’s expecting Tex-Mex chili, and that is not what you are signing up for!

When you’re playing dinner party DJ, what’s spinning?

There was a podcast I was obsessed with called The Dinner Party Download a decade ago, and I named my playlist after that. It has been evolving throughout the past 10 years and has Mitski, which I know feels sad for a dinner party but it’s mellow, some alt-J, Bill Withers, The Contours. A lot of Motown-era music, like The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, The Four Tops, Staple Singers. And then Janelle Monáe, Kate Nash, “Rhapsody in Blue” by George Gershwin is thrown in there. I go all over the place, but I think it creates a general buzzy atmosphere. I don’t want it to necessarily be as dancey as a dance party, but I also don’t want people to fall asleep, either.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

I really love plating things and cutting things into fun shapes and making them look pretty. I took a cooking class in Japan with Elizabeth Andoh, a very prolific cookbook writer, a couple of years ago, and after my fiancé and I walked out of it, we were just like, “Dang, our food’s real ugly!” A huge part of her class was how much presentation matters and how the first way that you are consuming the food is with your sight, with your eyes, so why not make it look cute?

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

While my fiancé and I were in Florence for a friend’s wedding, we knew that Italy, historically, was not the easiest place to be vegan. You can find things but maybe not that many things, and maybe not the things that look as good as the things everybody else is eating. So I was big sad the entire time until we stumbled into a tiny hole-in-the-wall vegan restaurant called Il Vegano. We found it on Google by searching “vegan restaurants near me,” and it had the best pasta with tomato sauce and tiramisù that either of us have ever had. Mind you, my fiancé is not vegan and very much could still eat real tiramisù and did on that trip. And the night ended with us essentially begging in broken Italian for the head chef to write a cookbook. We waddled back to our hotel saying it was the best meal we’ve ever had.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6459. How to Blind-Bake Pie Crust—and When You Need To

The road to pie perfection is paved in pitfalls. I’ve fallen into plenty of them throughout my baking career. The infamous “soggy bottom” is among the most common, but it’s easy to avoid. Blind baking—baking the crust before adding the filling—helps prevent an underbaked crust by giving the pastry a head start in the oven or cooking it completely before the filling goes in.

But getting the crust to the right color depends on what you’re planning to fill it with. A pale, partially baked shell might be perfect for one pie, while another needs a deep golden brown crust before you add even a spoonful of filling. Here’s how to know when enough color is enough.

Blind baking is especially useful when the filling needs less time in the oven than the crust does. For custard pies, like pumpkin pie, partially baking the shell gives the pastry a head start so it doesn’t end up uncooked beneath a set filling. For pies with no-bake fillings, such as chocolate pudding pie or cranberry curd pie, the crust needs to be fully baked before it’s filled.

Most traditional fruit pies don’t need blind baking. Their fillings and crusts spend enough time in the oven together for the pastry to cook through. There are exceptions, particularly single-crust fruit pies topped with a crumble. Our Peach-Blueberry Pie, for example, starts with a thoroughly blind-baked shell before the filling goes in. Follow your recipe’s instructions rather than assuming every fruit pie needs the same treatment.

Start with a good pie dough. Roll it out, fit it into the pie plate, and crimp the edge. Chill the shaped shell for at least 15 minutes before baking; cold dough holds its shape better in the oven, reducing the risk of shrinking or slumping.

Next, line the shell with parchment paper and fill it with pie weights. Crumpling the parchment first, then unfolding it, helps it conform to the shell. The weights hold the dough against the pan while it bakes, preventing the bottom from puffing up and the sides from collapsing.

You can buy ceramic pie weights or use dried beans, rice, or stainless-steel ball bearings. I’m partial to the ball bearings: They’re small enough to settle into the corners of the pie plate and heavy enough to hold the dough firmly in place.

Not everyone in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen agrees. Editors Jesse Szewczyk and Rebecca Firkser prefer lighter alternatives. In their experience, heavy metal weights can compress the dough, limiting the expansion of the buttery layers that make pie crust flaky. Jesse uses dried beans or rice; Rebecca prefers dried chickpeas or even granulated sugar, a technique popularized by baking expert Stella Parks.

All of these options can work. Whichever you choose, fill the parchment-lined shell generously, supporting the sides all the way to the rim. Leave the weights in place until the crust looks dry and set and the parchment releases easily; removing them too soon can cause the sides to slump.

Our Cranberry Meringue Pie has a fully blind-baked pie crust.

This method uses our Perfect Pie Crust dough and makes one 9"-diameter pie shell. It produces an evenly golden crust; if your pie calls for a paler or more deeply browned shell, follow its specific baking instructions and use the visual guide below.

Some pie recipes call for docking (pricking the bottom and sides of the dough with a fork) before baking. This allows steam to escape and helps prevent uneven puffing, but doesn’t replace the support of pie weights. Follow your recipe’s instructions; docking isn’t necessary for every blind-baked crust.

Do Ahead: A fully blind-baked crust can be made up to 2 days ahead. Let cool completely, wrap well, and store at room temperature until ready to fill.

The short answer: It depends on what you’re putting inside. Some pies need only a partially baked crust, while others call for a shell that’s deeply golden brown.

Oven temperatures vary, different pie plates conduct heat differently, and the filling determines how much additional baking the crust will get. Use the recipe’s timing as a guide, but watch the color and texture of the pastry. Here’s what to look for.

Fruit pies need a pale base because they bake a looong time. Or at least, that’s often the thinking. If you’re making a single-crust variety topped with a crumble, such as our Blueberry Crumble Pie, and the recipe calls for blind-baking, you might want to start with an anemic crust. It’ll have plenty of time to brown as the juices thicken.

A pale, partially baked crust should look set rather than raw. The bottom should look set and opaque with some light golden patches, while the crimped edge may already be noticeably browned. The crust will continue to develop color once the filling goes in.

Don’t assume fruit pies always need a pale shell. Our Peach-Blueberry Pie, for example, calls for a well-browned crust before the fruit and crumble go in. And many double-crust fruit pies don’t need blind baking at all.

A lightly baked shell can also be appropriate for custards that have a substantial bake ahead. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie starts with a partially baked crust before the custard goes in for at least another hour.

The goal is to give the crust enough of a head start without taking it so far that the edges burn before the filling finishes cooking.

Custard pies, such as chess and our Lemon Buttermilk Pie, often have shorter bake times than fruit pies, so the crust needs a solid golden base layer to develop enough color by the time the filling sets.

Here, you’re looking for more than a crust that’s simply dry and set. The bottom should be evenly golden with no pale, translucent patches, and the sides should have taken on some color too. The rim will generally be a little darker than the bottom, but the whole shell should look well on its way to being fully baked.

Our Perfect Pie Crust recipe produces this kind of shell. It calls for baking the weighted crust until the edges are golden, then removing the weights and continuing until the bottom and sides are evenly browned.

And some pies need an even more substantial head start. Our Bourbon-Date Pecan Pie takes the crust to a dry golden finish before adding a filling that bakes for another 45–55 minutes.

The point isn’t that every custard pie needs the same color. It’s that the crust should be baked far enough that it won’t be left pale and doughy by the time the filling is done.

Bake the crust to a dark golden brown if you’re adding a no-bake filling, like a pudding or curd. You’re going for a toasty, burnished color, so don’t be gun-shy.

Because the filling won’t return to the oven, this is the crust’s one chance to bake all the way through. You want deep color across the entire bottom and up the sides—not just a dark rim surrounding a pale center. The pastry should look dry, crisp, and well browned, without any doughy or translucent spots.

After removing the pie weights, continue baking until the shell is fully browned, checking frequently toward the end. Depending on the dough and oven temperature, that might take another 15–20 minutes or longer. Don’t pull it simply because the timer has gone off.

Our Cranberry Meringue Pie uses this approach: The crust is baked until golden and dry before the cranberry curd filling goes in. A fully baked shell develops a richer, toastier flavor and is better equipped to stand up to a moist filling.

Some recipes, including our pumpkin pie, call for brushing a thin layer of beaten egg onto the partially baked shell and returning it to the oven briefly to set. This, ostensibly, creates a barrier between the pastry and the filling, but not all bakers believe the hype.

While it can be a useful extra precaution, it is by no means a universal requirement. If your recipe doesn’t call for it, there’s no need to add another step.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published in May 2016 and has been updated with additional reporting and expanded instructions by Phoebe Fry.

#6458. Flambéed French Onion Crêpes

“As much as I appreciate a classic like crêpes Suzette, I also love a cheeky little twist!” says New York City pastry chef and cookbook author Caroline Schiff. Here, she takes the traditional dessert on a 180-degree ride to the savory side and nods to another classic along the way: French onion soup. She ditches the citrusy butter sauce in favor of golden caramelized onions and gloriously gooey gruyère, but keeps the drama by adding a splash of sherry and igniting it before serving.

Featured in “Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?” by Ellery Weil.

#6457. Wendy’s Brought Back A Beloved Piece Of Its Past—Plus Two New Holiday Frostys

All I want for Christmas is my old Wendy’s sunroom back.

Wendy’s is getting nostalgic this holiday season, and as someone who grew up eating in one of the chain’s iconic glass sunrooms, I’m particularly excited about this one.

The fast food chain just launched a limited-time Holiday Box complete with retro packaging, collectible knit hats, and a choice of some familiar menu favorites. And of course, two new peppermint-inspired Frosty desserts.

Obviously, I had to try everything for myself.

Available beginning November 16 at participating Wendy’s locations nationwide, the Holiday Box starts at $11.99 and includes your choice of a Dave’s Double or 10-piece crispy or spicy chicken nuggets, small fries, a small soft drink, and one collectible knit hat.

The packaging is designed to resemble Wendy’s old-school Solarium restaurants, complete with the recognizable glass-walled dining area that became a staple of the chain beginning in the 1980s.

And I have to admit, this one hit me right in the childhood memories.

Growing up, I remember going to Wendy’s with my mom and sitting in that yellow, glass-enclosed sunroom. Seeing the design recreated as a miniature holiday box immediately brought me back to those visits.

Each Holiday Box includes one of four collectible knit hats featuring a retro Wendy’s design: Frosty, Biggie, the classic Wendy’s logo, or the famous “Where’s the Beef?” slogan.

The hats come in sealed mystery bags, meaning you won’t know which one you’re getting until you open it.

Thankfully, I ended up with the blue Frosty beanie, which was exactly the design I was hoping for.

Had I opened the bag to find a hat with “Biggie” written across my forehead, though, I think we would’ve had a problem.

The Holiday Box is available for a limited time while supplies last, and customers can’t select which hat they receive.

Alongside the Holiday Box, Wendy’s is introducing two limited-time desserts: the Peppermint Frosty Swirl and Peppermint Brownie Frosty Fusion.

Both are available with either a vanilla or chocolate Frosty base, so I decided to try one of each.

The Peppermint Brownie Frosty Fusion combines Wendy’s classic Frosty with peppermint sauce and brownie pieces, creating a dessert that feels especially appropriate for the holiday season.

I went with the vanilla base, and I absolutely loved it.

The peppermint flavor was strong and immediately reminded me of a candy cane or a York Peppermint Pattie. It had that recognizable minty sweetness I look for in a holiday dessert, without getting lost in the vanilla Frosty.

The brownie pieces were another highlight, adding a nice texture and a layer of chocolate flavor to the mix. I particularly liked how the chocolate complemented the peppermint rather than competing with it.

For me, this is exactly what a seasonal Frosty should taste like. It’s festive, flavorful, and different enough from the regular menu to make it worth trying.

For my second dessert, I went with the chocolate Peppermint Frosty Swirl, which combines Wendy’s classic Chocolate Frosty with peppermint sauce.

My biggest piece of advice is to give this one a good stir before digging in.

When I first tried it, most of the peppermint syrup was concentrated toward the top of the dessert. Mixing everything together helped distribute the flavor more evenly throughout the Frosty.

The combination of chocolate and peppermint works well, although I didn’t find the mint flavor nearly as strong as it was in the vanilla Brownie Frosty Fusion.

Still, I’m happy to report that Wendy’s peppermint sauce works with both Frosty flavors. If you prefer a more straightforward chocolate-mint combination without brownie pieces, this is a solid option.

Personally, though, I’d go back for the Fusion.

This tiny inkwell contains an alphabetic inscription in ancient Etruscan, a language that has never been fully decoded.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell

This small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

The vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

According to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet shows that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#6454. Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, New York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.)

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, said that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”

Part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit New York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she says. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, says that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to new takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she says. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, New York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.)

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, said that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”

Part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit New York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she says. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, says that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to new takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she says. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

#6452. BA's Best Pecan Pie

Our classic pecan pie recipe has no chocolate chips, no booze, and no hard-to-find ingredients. Instead of focusing on embellishments, we focused on what matters most: the deep flavor of toasted pecans, a caramelly custard, and a buttery, flaky pie crust.

Brown sugar and a spoonful of dark molasses add depth to the filling, while toasting the pecans before incorporating them makes their flavor stand out and their texture more robust. Blind baking the crust—baking it before adding the filling—helps keep the bottom crisp beneath the gooey custard.

When the pie comes out of the oven, the edges should be set and slightly puffed, but the center should still wobble like Jell-O. It will continue to set as it cools, so resist slicing too soon. Serve it all on its own, or gild it with vanilla ice cream or whipped cream.

Can I make this pecan pie without corn syrup?

Yes. Corn syrup gives this classic pie its perfectly gooey texture, but there are alternatives. Brown rice syrup will add a toasty flavor and can be used in equal parts. Golden syrup, honey, and maple syrup are all too sweet and will change the pie’s flavor and texture.

For a pie developed without any syrup, try our Bourbon-Date Pecan Pie.

Can I use chopped pecans instead of halves?

Yes. We love the crunch you get from pecan halves, but if you’re a chopped pecan person, use about 225 g in place of the 2 cups of halves. Watch closely when toasting; chopped pecans will need less time in the oven.

Yes—bake the pie a day ahead and refrigerate it. Let it cool on a rack for up to 2 hours, then transfer it to the refrigerator to finish cooling before covering. To get a head start on the pastry, refrigerate the dough for up to 3 days or freeze it for up to 2 months.

Pulse 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 2 cups all-purpose flour in a food processor until combined. Add 5 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 3 Tbsp. chilled lard or vegetable shortening and pulse until mixture resembles coarse meal with a few pieces of butter and lard visible, about fifteen 1-second pulses. With motor running, drizzle in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar and 5½ Tbsp. ice water and pulse until dough is still crumbly but just holds together when squeezed (add 1 tsp. water at a time if necessary, but be careful not to overwork dough).

Turn out dough onto a work surface. Knead 1–2 times, pressing just to incorporate any shaggy pieces. Flatten into a 6"-wide disk. Wrap with plastic wrap and chill at least 1 hour.

Preheat oven to 425°. Roll out dough on a lightly floured work surface to a 14" round. Transfer to a 9" pie pan. Pick up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish, letting excess dough hang over dish. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Fold overhang under; pinch and crimp. Chill 30 minutes.

Line dough with parchment paper or foil, leaving some overhang. Fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until crust is dry around the edges and just beginning to lightly brown, 25–35 minutes. Carefully remove parchment and weights and reduce oven temperature to 350°. Bake until crust is set and beginning to brown in the center, 10–15 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 3 days ahead; keep chilled, or freeze up to 2 months. Crust can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and store at room temperature.

Preheat oven to 350°. Toast 2 cups (225 g) pecan halves on a rimmed baking sheet until browned and fragrant, 8–10 minutes. Let cool.

Reduce oven temperature to 325°. Whisk 4 large eggs, room temperature, beaten to blend, 1 cup light corn syrup, ⅔ cup (packed; 134 g) light brown sugar, 1 Tbsp. robust-flavored (dark) molasses, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Slowly whisk in 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, until combined. Fold in pecans and pour into cooled crust.

Bake pie until edges are set and slightly puffed but center is recessed and wobbles like Jell-O, 55–70 minutes (it will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack and let cool at least 3 hours before slicing. Serve with vanilla ice cream.

Do Ahead: Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and chill. Serve warm or at room temperature.

#6451. Lucid Dreaming Was Once a Rare Gift. Now Scientists Say They Can Help You Learn It.

Researchers built dreamlike virtual worlds to teach people how to realize they’re dreaming—and it worked.

Some people don’t just dream. They often realize they’re dreaming and can even control the dreamworld, from giving themselves powers that defy the laws of physics to escaping a nightmare by waking themselves up. Lucid dreamers can go on adventures most of us can only dream about (pun intended). But is it possible to train yourself to do the same?

Dreams can happen during any stage of sleep, but they usually occur during REM sleep. When dreamers suddenly become aware that they’re dreaming, they’re in a lucid state. However, people who frequently have lucid dreams are rare. Researchers from the University of Trento in Rovereto, Italy, wanted to find out whether standard exercises, meditation, and virtual reality could teach people to have lucid dreams. Participants in the experimental group practiced open monitoring meditation, which is meant to sharpen sensory awareness and perception through nonjudgmental observation. They then did VR training that took them into virtual worlds full of bizarre, dreamlike scenarios. For comparison, a control group used VR that had nothing to do with dreaming, while a third group did only the standard training, without VR.

All participants started with the same baseline training, which they did while awake to practice dream recall and reality checks. They were told to keep a dream diary, noting each morning whether they remembered any dreams and, if so, what the dreams were about. Participants were also told to do reality checks, such as pinching themselves, to test whether they were awake or dreaming. They did these checks whenever they ran into something strange or simply thought of something strange. On top of that, phone alarms went off every hour for 12 hours each day to prompt more checks. The idea was that the habit would eventually carry over into their dreams. On top of this training, the experimental group did open monitoring meditation sessions in the lab to prepare for their VR training. During these sessions, participants observed their breathing, bodily sensations, thoughts, and emotions without reacting to them. Each session also included a guided exploration of an environment designed to look like a scene from a dream.

“Through repetition, [reality checks] are intended to become habitual and to transfer into dreams via ‘dream residue,’ where they may be triggered by dream signs that are unusual, surprising, or incongruent events, and thereby precipitate insight into the dream state,” the researchers wrote in their study, recently published in Frontiers in Psychology.

To build these scenes, the researchers created LucidDreamingVR, a program inspired by Tibetan dream yoga. Unlike the VR control group, whose content had nothing to do with dreaming, the experimental group completed eight sessions that grew steadily more elaborate, taking participants from recognizing a dream to controlling one. The early tasks taught them to spot dream signs: the virtual surroundings would suddenly shift, cueing a reality check, much as an odd detail might inside a dream. Later sessions drew on dream yoga techniques to let participants rehearse what they might do once they became lucid. With a single spoken command, they could fly, leap to incredible heights or, like Alice after tumbling down the rabbit hole, grow and shrink at will.

The researchers counted both lucid and semi-lucid dreams as “lucid-like” dreams. By the end of the experiment, 11 of the 13 participants who had trained with LucidDreamingVR had reported at least one lucid-like dream. By contrast, eight of 13 people in the control group without VR and only four of 12 in the VR control group reported one. Nearly 12% of the dreams the experimental group remembered were lucid-like, compared with about 3% for the control group without VR and about 1% for the VR control group. Surprisingly, the LucidDreamingVR group remembered the fewest dreams overall, so they also reported the fewest ordinary, non-lucid dreams. These results suggest that combining open monitoring meditation with dream-themed VR may increase lucid dreaming. However, because neither control group meditated, the study can’t show which part of the training mattered more.

“[Our] findings support the use of immersive environments as…cognitive-enhancement tools,” the researchers said. “Future work should combine VR-based rehearsal with objective sleep verification, factorial designs, and waking cognitive measures to clarify mechanism, specificity, and transfer.”

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a new study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

However, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

Of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at New York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus said.

It's important to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

The "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus said. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, said in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites."

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes."

Weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an important question for future research."

Snyder, T. J., & Klaus, H. D. (2026). Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 5, 1889466. https://doi.org/10.3389/fearc.2026.1889466

He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.
